# Basic Matrix Operations {#sec-matrix}

Python/numpy/scipy provide a range of options for achieving basic matrix operations. You will need to take a little care to ensure that your code implements the operations you intend it to. This is largely due to the fact that some operators/functions will change their behaviour depending on the input you provide. This section includes some recommendations for simple linear algebra, which should ensure your code behaves as desired.

For further information, look at the reference pages : 
[https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/routines.array-manipulation.html](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/routines.array-manipulation.html)
[https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/routines.linalg.html](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/routines.linalg.html)
and



## Matrix representation

Matrices can be implemented as a 2D `np.ndarray`. Basic matrix arithmetic can then be performed using standard operators `+`,`-` and `@`. 

```{python}
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1, 2, 3,],[4, 5, 6],[1, 0, 0]])
B = np.array([[1, 0, 0,],[0, 1, 0],[0, 0, 1]])

# addition
print(A + B)

# subtraction
print(A - B)

# scalar multiplication
print(3*B)

# matrix multiplication
print(np.matmul(A, B))
print(A @ B)
```

The transpose of a matrix is given by `np.transpose()` or `ndarray.T`.

## Vector representation

Vectors can be implemented as 1D arrays, or as 2D arrays. A 1D array will be interpreted as row or column vector depending on the context in which it is used. Use of 2D arrays allows you to specify row or column form. This can be useful, since `np.matmul()` or `@` will throw an exception if you accidentally try to perform an illegal matrix operation.

```{python}
v  = np.array([1,2,3])
vr = np.array([[1,2,3]])
vc = np.array([[1],[2],[3]])

# two options for matrix * vector
print(A@v)
print(A@vc)

# two options for vector * matrix
print(v@A)
print(vr@A)

# this is not a valid matrix multiplication !
print(A@vr)
```

## Vector and Matrix Products

The usual vector dot and cross products are provided by 
`np.vdot()`, `np.cross()`.  The inner and outer products are provided by `np.inner()` and `np.outer()`.

The matrix product is provided by `np.matmul()` or the `@` operator. Numpy will also perform matrix multiplication with `np.dot()`, but it is not recommended if you can use `@` or `np.matmul()`.

## Norms {#sec-norms}

A norm is a function that assigns a single non-negative number to a vector (or matrix), intended to represent its "size" or "length".  This is a generalisation of the vector magnitude, defined as the square root of the sum of the squares of its components.  This is known as the Euclidean norm or L2 norm.  We can define other norms, which have different properties and uses.  For a vector $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)$, the most commonly used norms are:

<!-- Norms come up throughout machine learning: they measure how large a set of model weights is (used in regularisation, @sec-supervised-ml), how large a gradient is (used in gradient clipping, @sec-optimisation), and how far apart two vectors are (used in nearest-neighbour methods and clustering, @sec-unsupervised-ml). -->

$$
\|\mathbf{x}\|_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i| \qquad \text{(L1 / "Manhattan" norm)}
$$

$$
\|\mathbf{x}\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2} \qquad \text{(L2 / Euclidean norm)}
$$

$$
\|\mathbf{x}\|_\infty = \max_i |x_i| \qquad \text{(max / Chebyshev norm)}
$$

Matrices also have norms. The most commonly used is the Frobenius norm, which simply treats the matrix as a long vector of all its entries:

$$
\|A\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i,j} a_{ij}^2}
$$

```{python}
import numpy as np

x = np.array([3., -4., 1.])
print("L1 norm  :", np.linalg.norm(x, ord=1))
print("L2 norm  :", np.linalg.norm(x, ord=2))
print("Max norm :", np.linalg.norm(x, ord=np.inf))

A = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
print("Frobenius norm :", np.linalg.norm(A, ord='fro'))
```

## Rank {#sec-rank}

The rank of a matrix $A$ is the number of linearly independent rows (equivalently, columns) it contains. For an $m \times n$ matrix, the rank can be at most $\min(m,n)$; if it achieves this maximum it is called full rank, otherwise it is rank-deficient.

```{python}
A_full = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 5.]])
A_deficient = np.array([[1., 2.], [2., 4.]])   # second row is 2x the first

print("Rank of full-rank matrix      :", np.linalg.matrix_rank(A_full))
print("Rank of rank-deficient matrix :", np.linalg.matrix_rank(A_deficient))
```

The rank of a matrix is related to the solvability of $Ax=y$. If $A$ is full rank, the equation has a unique solution. When $A$ is rank-deficient, an exact solution may not exist and other approaches must be used, as discussed in @sec-sim-eqn.  A rank deficient matrix must also have at least one zero eigenvalue, which is why $\det(A)=0$ when $A$ is not invertible.

## Other matrix operations

Finally, `scipy.linalg` provides some additional basic operations such as the determinant and the inverse.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import scipy.linalg as linalg

A = np.array([[1, 2, 3,],[4, 5, 6],[1, 0, 0]])
detA = linalg.det(A)
print(detA)

invA = linalg.inv(A)
print(invA)
```


<!-- ### Why this matters for training

When training a neural network (@sec-nn), the gradient of the loss with respect to all the weights can occasionally become very large — for example early in training, or with recurrent networks over long sequences (@sec-rnn). If left unchecked, a single large gradient step can destabilise training. A standard mitigation, **gradient clipping**, simply rescales the gradient vector if its norm exceeds some threshold $\tau$:

$$
\mathbf{g} \leftarrow \mathbf{g} \times \min\left(1, \frac{\tau}{\|\mathbf{g}\|_2}\right)
$$

This is a direct, practical use of the L2 norm defined above, and is worth keeping in mind when we return to gradient descent in @sec-optimisation. -->
